strings.b-00-meta.title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.0: After this lesson you can describe the magnetic field of a magnet and its field lines, and list the properties of field lines.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.1: After this lesson you can find the direction of the magnetic field produced by a current in a straight wire, in a circular loop and in a solenoid, using the right-hand thumb rule.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.2: After this lesson you can use Fleming's left-hand rule to find the direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.3: After this lesson you can describe the wires, the safety devices and the common faults of a domestic electric circuit.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.0.definition: The region around a magnet in which the force of the magnet can be detected; it has both direction and magnitude.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.1.definition: A smooth curve drawn with the help of iron filings or a compass needle showing the direction of the magnetic field; lines emerge from the north pole, merge at the south pole and never cross.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.2.definition: Point the thumb of your right hand along the current in a straight conductor; your curled fingers then show the direction of the magnetic field lines.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.3.definition: A coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wound in the shape of a cylinder; its field is like that of a bar magnet and is uniform inside.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.4.definition: A soft iron core wrapped with a coil of insulated copper wire, which becomes a strong magnet when current flows through the coil.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.5.definition: First finger along the magnetic field, second finger along the current, thumb along the force on the conductor.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.6.definition: The domestic supply wire with red insulation, also called the positive wire.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.7.definition: The domestic supply wire with black insulation, also called the negative wire; the potential difference between live and neutral is 220 V.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.8.definition: The green-insulated wire connected to a metal plate deep in the earth, giving a low-resistance path so that a leakage current does not give a severe shock.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.9.definition: Direct contact between the live and neutral wires (damaged insulation or a faulty appliance) that makes the current abruptly increase.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.10.definition: A condition where the current in a circuit becomes too large, from short-circuiting, a hike in supply voltage, or too many appliances on one socket.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.11.definition: A safety device that melts by Joule heating and breaks the circuit when the current is too large.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.0: A current in a wire can heat the wire, but it can do something else too. A wire carrying an electric current behaves like a magnet.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.1: Connect a straight thick copper wire between two points X and Y of a circuit, keeping the wire perpendicular to the plane of the paper. Place a small compass horizontally near the wire, note the position of its needle, then insert the key and pass a current. The needle is deflected.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.2: The deflection means that the electric current through the copper wire has produced a magnetic effect. So electricity and magnetism are linked to each other.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.3: Hans Christian Oersted, one of the leading scientists of the 19th century, found this in 1820. He accidentally discovered that a compass needle got deflected when an electric current passed through a metallic wire placed nearby, and through this observation he showed that electricity and magnetism were related phenomena. The unit of magnetic field strength is named the oersted in his honour.
strings.b-02.question: A compass needle placed near a straight copper wire is deflected when the key is inserted and current flows. What does this show?
strings.b-02.options.0: The copper wire has become a permanent magnet.
strings.b-02.options.1: The electric current through the wire has produced a magnetic effect.
strings.b-02.options.2: The compass needle has lost its magnetism.
strings.b-02.options.3: The current in the wire has stopped.
strings.b-02.explanation: The needle is deflected only while the current flows, so the current itself is producing a magnetic field around the wire. That is why electricity and magnetism are said to be linked.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.0: A compass needle gets deflected when brought near a bar magnet. A compass needle is, in fact, a small bar magnet: its ends point approximately towards north and south. The end pointing towards north is called the north-seeking or north pole, and the other end, pointing towards south, is the south-seeking or south pole.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.1: Fix a sheet of white paper on a drawing board and place a bar magnet at the centre. Sprinkle iron filings uniformly around the magnet, using a salt-sprinkler if you like, and tap the board gently. The filings arrange themselves in a pattern, because the magnet exerts its influence in the region surrounding it and the filings experience a force. The region surrounding a magnet, in which the force of the magnet can be detected, is said to have a magnetic field. The lines along which the iron filings align themselves represent magnetic field lines.
strings.b-04.paragraphs.0: You can draw the field lines yourself with a small compass and a bar magnet. Place the magnet on a sheet of paper fixed on a drawing board and mark the boundary of the magnet. Place the compass near the north pole: the south pole of the needle points towards the north pole of the magnet, and the north pole of the compass is directed away from it.
strings.b-04.paragraphs.1: Mark the position of the two ends of the needle. Now move the compass to a new position such that its south pole occupies the position previously occupied by its north pole. Proceed step by step till you reach the south pole of the magnet. Join the points marked on the paper by a smooth curve: this curve represents a field line. Repeat the procedure and draw as many lines as you can; the pattern you get is the magnetic field around the magnet. As you move the needle along a field line towards the poles, the deflection increases.
strings.b-05.caption: Field lines around a bar magnet. They emerge from the north pole, loop round outside, and merge at the south pole; the arrowheads show the direction in which the north pole of a compass needle would move. Inside the magnet the direction is from south pole to north pole, so the lines are closed curves.
strings.b-05.svg_texts.t-1: lines are crowded near the poles, where the field is stronger
strings.b-06.paragraphs.0: Magnetic field is a quantity that has both direction and magnitude. The direction of the magnetic field at a point is taken to be the direction in which a north pole of the compass needle moves inside it. So by convention, field lines emerge from the north pole and merge at the south pole. Inside the magnet the direction of field lines is from its south pole to its north pole. Thus magnetic field lines are closed curves.
strings.b-06.paragraphs.1: The relative strength of the magnetic field is shown by the degree of closeness of the field lines. The field is stronger, that is, the force acting on the pole of another magnet placed there is greater, where the field lines are crowded.
strings.b-06.paragraphs.2: No two field lines cross each other. If they did, it would mean that at the point of intersection the compass needle would point towards two directions, which is not possible.
strings.b-06.paragraphs.3: Weak magnetic fields are present in our bodies too. Ion currents along nerve cells produce temporary fields about one-billionth of the earth's magnetic field. The heart and the brain produce significant fields, and the magnetic field inside the body is the basis of obtaining images of body parts by a technique called Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI).
strings.b-07.question: Why does a compass needle get deflected when brought near a bar magnet?
strings.b-07.options.0: The needle is a small bar magnet, and the magnetic field of the bar magnet exerts a force on it.
strings.b-07.options.1: The bar magnet heats the needle.
strings.b-07.options.2: Air pressure pushes the needle aside.
strings.b-07.explanation: A compass needle is itself a small bar magnet. Inside the magnetic field of the bar magnet it experiences a force, so it turns and its ends point along the field lines.
strings.b-08.question: Which one of the following is NOT a property of magnetic field lines?
strings.b-08.options.0: They emerge from the north pole and merge at the south pole.
strings.b-08.options.1: They are crowded where the magnetic field is stronger.
strings.b-08.options.2: They cross one another near the poles.
strings.b-08.explanation: No two field lines are found to cross each other. If they did, then at the point of intersection the compass needle would point towards two directions at the same time, which is not possible.
strings.b-09.title: How to draw a magnetic field line with a compass
strings.b-09.steps.0.title: Fix the paper and the magnet
strings.b-09.steps.0.detail: Place a bar magnet on a sheet of white paper fixed on a drawing board, and mark the boundary of the magnet.
strings.b-09.steps.1.title: Start near the north pole
strings.b-09.steps.1.detail: Place the compass near the north pole of the magnet. The south pole of the needle points towards the magnet's north pole, and the needle's north pole is directed away from it.
strings.b-09.steps.2.title: Mark the needle
strings.b-09.steps.2.detail: Mark on the paper the position of the two ends of the needle.
strings.b-09.steps.3.title: Move the needle onwards
strings.b-09.steps.3.detail: Move the compass to a new position such that its south pole occupies the position previously occupied by its north pole.
strings.b-09.steps.4.title: Walk to the south pole
strings.b-09.steps.4.detail: Go on step by step in this way till you reach the south pole of the magnet.
strings.b-09.steps.5.title: Join the marks
strings.b-09.steps.5.detail: Join the points marked on the paper by a smooth curve. This curve represents a field line. Repeat the whole procedure and draw as many lines as you can.
strings.b-10.paragraphs.0: Pass a current through a long straight thick copper wire held vertically, and sprinkle iron filings uniformly on a cardboard through which the wire passes. Tapping the cardboard gently makes the filings arrange themselves in a pattern of concentric circles around the copper wire. These concentric circles represent the magnetic field lines.
strings.b-10.paragraphs.1: Place a compass at a point on one circle. The direction of the north pole of the compass needle gives the direction of the field line at that point, and you can show this direction by an arrow. If the direction of the current through the straight wire is reversed, the direction of the magnetic field lines is also reversed.
strings.b-11.caption: The field around a straight current-carrying wire is a set of concentric circles centred on the wire. The arrowheads give the direction of the field; reversing the current reverses them. The circles get larger as we move away from the wire, where the field is weaker.
strings.b-11.svg_texts.t-1: the wire is seen end on: current comes out of the page
strings.b-12.title: Field of a straight wire: change the current, change the distance
strings.b-12.description: A straight wire is seen end on, with a compass placed at a chosen distance from it. The concentric field circles are drawn around the wire. Increase the current and the needle turns further; move the compass farther away and the turn becomes smaller. The turn of the needle is shown in words only (small, medium, large), because the chapter tells us only that the deflection increases with current and decreases with distance, not by how much.
strings.b-12.controls.current.label: Current in the wire (A)
strings.b-12.controls.distance.label: Distance of the compass from the wire (steps)
strings.b-12.controls.direction.label: Direction of current (out of page = 1, into page = -1)
strings.b-13.paragraphs.0: What happens to the deflection of a compass needle placed at a given point if the current in the copper wire is changed? Vary the current and watch. If the current is increased, the deflection also increases. This indicates that the magnitude of the magnetic field produced at a given point increases as the current through the wire increases.
strings.b-13.paragraphs.1: What happens if the compass is moved away from the copper wire while the current stays the same? Place the compass at a farther point. The deflection in the needle decreases. Thus the magnetic field produced by a given current in the conductor decreases as the distance from it increases, and the concentric circles representing the field around a current-carrying straight wire become larger and larger as we move away from it.
strings.b-14.question: Which of the following correctly describes the magnetic field near a long straight wire?
strings.b-14.options.0: The field consists of straight lines perpendicular to the wire.
strings.b-14.options.1: The field consists of straight lines parallel to the wire.
strings.b-14.options.2: The field consists of radial lines originating from the wire.
strings.b-14.options.3: The field consists of concentric circles centred on the wire.
strings.b-14.explanation: Iron filings sprinkled on a cardboard through which the wire passes settle along concentric circles around the wire, so the field lines near a long straight current-carrying wire are concentric circles centred on the wire.
strings.b-15.question: In the activity with a straight copper wire lying parallel to and over a compass needle, the current flows from north to south and the north pole of the needle moves towards the east. The current is now made to flow from south to north. The north pole of the needle will move towards the
strings.b-15.explanation: Reversing the direction of the current through the wire reverses the direction of the magnetic field produced by it, so the needle is deflected the opposite way — towards the west.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.0: Here is a convenient way of finding the direction of the magnetic field associated with a current-carrying conductor. Imagine that you are holding a current-carrying straight conductor in your right hand such that the thumb points towards the direction of the current. Then your fingers will wrap around the conductor in the direction of the field lines of the magnetic field. This is known as the right-hand thumb rule.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.1: This rule is also called Maxwell's corkscrew rule. If we consider ourselves driving a corkscrew in the direction of the current, then the direction of the rotation of the corkscrew is the direction of the magnetic field.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.2: Use it like this: first fix the direction of the current with your thumb, then read the direction of the field from the way your fingers curl. The field circles lie in planes perpendicular to the wire.
strings.b-17.problem: A current through a horizontal power line flows in east to west direction. What is the direction of magnetic field at a point directly below it and at a point directly above it?
strings.b-17.steps.0.title: Note the direction of the current
strings.b-17.steps.0.detail: The power line is horizontal and the current flows from east to west.
strings.b-17.steps.1.title: Apply the right-hand thumb rule
strings.b-17.steps.1.detail: Hold the wire in your right hand with the thumb pointing along the current, from east to west. Your fingers then curl around the wire in the direction of the magnetic field.
strings.b-17.steps.2.title: Picture the field circles
strings.b-17.steps.2.detail: The field lines are circles lying in a plane perpendicular to the wire, that is, in a vertical plane running north-south. The field at a point directly below the wire and at a point directly above the wire both lie on these circles.
strings.b-17.steps.3.title: Read off the sense of turning
strings.b-17.steps.3.detail: Looking along the wire from the east end, the curling of the fingers — and so the field — turns clockwise; looking from the west end, the same field turns anti-clockwise.
strings.b-17.answer: The magnetic field at any point below or above the wire turns clockwise in a plane perpendicular to the wire when viewed from the east end, and anti-clockwise when viewed from the west end.
strings.b-18.question: A long straight wire carries a current vertically upwards. Using the right-hand thumb rule, the magnetic field lines around the wire are
strings.b-18.options.0: straight lines parallel to the wire.
strings.b-18.options.1: circles around the wire, running anticlockwise when seen from above.
strings.b-18.options.2: circles around the wire, running clockwise when seen from above.
strings.b-18.options.3: radial lines spreading out from the wire.
strings.b-18.explanation: Point the thumb of your right hand upwards along the current; your fingers curl around the wire. Seen from above, that curl is anticlockwise.
strings.b-19.paragraphs.0: Suppose the straight wire is bent in the form of a circular loop and a current is passed through it. The magnetic field produced by a current-carrying straight wire depends inversely on the distance from it, so at every point of the loop the circles representing the field become larger and larger as we move away from the wire.
strings.b-19.paragraphs.1: By the time we reach the centre of the circular loop, the arcs of these big circles appear as straight lines. Every point on the wire carrying current gives rise to a magnetic field that appears as a straight line at the centre of the loop. Applying the right-hand rule, it is easy to check that every section of the wire contributes to the magnetic field lines in the same direction within the loop.
strings.b-20.caption: A circular loop seen edge on, so that the wire is cut at two places marked A and B. The field lines around each piece of wire are circles; between A and B both fields point upwards, which is why every section of the loop adds to the field in the same direction inside the loop.
strings.b-20.svg_texts.t-0: both fields point the same way
strings.b-20.svg_texts.t-1: A: current out of the page    B: current into the page
strings.b-21.question: A circular loop of wire lies in the plane of the table and the current flows clockwise when seen from above. The magnetic field at the centre of the loop is
strings.b-21.options.0: in the plane of the table, pointing outwards from the centre.
strings.b-21.options.1: perpendicular to the table, pointing downwards into the table.
strings.b-21.options.2: perpendicular to the table, pointing upwards.
strings.b-21.options.3: zero at the centre of the loop.
strings.b-21.explanation: Apply the right-hand rule to the loop: curl your fingers in the direction of the current, which is clockwise seen from above, and the thumb points away from you — downwards into the table. So the field inside the loop is perpendicular to the table, pointing downwards, and outside the loop it points the other way.
strings.b-22.paragraphs.0: The magnetic field produced by a current-carrying wire at a given point depends directly on the current passing through it. Therefore, if there is a circular coil having n turns, the field produced is n times as large as that produced by a single turn. This is because the current in each circular turn has the same direction, and the field due to each turn then just adds up.
strings.b-22.paragraphs.1: A solenoid is a coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wound in the shape of a cylinder. Its magnetic field lines are like those of a bar magnet: one end of the solenoid acts as a magnetic north pole. The field lines inside the solenoid are parallel straight lines, and the magnetic field is uniform — the same at all points — inside a long solenoid carrying current.
strings.b-22.paragraphs.2: A strong magnetic field inside a current-carrying solenoid is used to magnetise a piece of steel placed inside it. An electromagnet consists of a core of soft iron wrapped around with a coil of insulated copper wire.
strings.b-23.caption: Field lines of a current-carrying solenoid. Inside the coil they are parallel straight lines, so the field there is uniform; outside they loop from one end to the other, just as they do round a bar magnet, and one end of the solenoid acts as a magnetic north pole.
strings.b-23.svg_texts.t-0: inside the solenoid the field lines are parallel straight lines
strings.b-24.question: Choose the correct option. The magnetic field inside a long straight solenoid carrying current
strings.b-24.options.1: decreases as we move towards its end.
strings.b-24.options.2: increases as we move towards its end.
strings.b-24.options.3: is the same at all points.
strings.b-24.explanation: The field lines inside a long current-carrying solenoid are parallel straight lines, evenly spaced, so the field is uniform — the same at all points inside it.
strings.b-25.paragraphs.0: An electric current flowing through a conductor produces a magnetic field, and the field so produced exerts a force on a magnet placed in the vicinity of the conductor. The French scientist Andre Marie Ampere suggested that the magnet must also exert an equal and opposite force on the current-carrying conductor.
strings.b-25.paragraphs.1: Suspend a small aluminium rod AB, about 5 cm long, horizontally from a stand using two connecting wires. Place a strong horse-shoe magnet so that the rod lies between the two poles with the magnetic field directed upwards: the north pole vertically below and the south pole vertically above the rod. Connect the rod in series with a battery, a key and a rheostat, and pass a current through the rod from end B to end A. The rod is displaced. Reverse the direction of the current and the rod is displaced in the opposite direction.
strings.b-25.paragraphs.2: Now interchange the two poles of the magnet so that the field is vertically downwards. Once again the direction of the force acting on the current-carrying rod gets reversed. This shows that the direction of the force on the conductor depends upon the direction of the current and the direction of the magnetic field.
strings.b-26.paragraphs.0: Experiments have shown that the displacement of the rod is largest, that is, the magnitude of the force is the highest, when the direction of the current is at right angles to the direction of the magnetic field. In such a condition we can use a simple rule to find the direction of the force on the conductor.
strings.b-26.paragraphs.1: The rule is Fleming's left-hand rule. Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of your left hand such that they are mutually perpendicular. If the first finger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the second finger in the direction of the current, then the thumb will point in the direction of motion, or the force acting on the conductor.
strings.b-26.paragraphs.2: Devices that use current-carrying conductors and magnetic fields include the electric motor, the electric generator, loudspeakers, microphones and measuring instruments.
strings.b-27.caption: Fleming's left-hand rule. The three directions are mutually perpendicular: the first finger points along the magnetic field, the second finger along the current, and the thumb along the force (or motion) on the conductor.
strings.b-28.problem: An electron enters a magnetic field at right angles to it. The direction of force acting on the electron will be (a) to the right. (b) to the left. (c) out of the page. (d) into the page.
strings.b-28.steps.0.title: Fix the direction of the current
strings.b-28.steps.0.detail: The direction of current is taken opposite to the direction of motion of electrons. So first turn the electron's direction of motion round by half a turn to get the direction of the current.
strings.b-28.steps.1.title: Note the angle between current and field
strings.b-28.steps.1.detail: The electron enters at right angles to the field, so the current is also at right angles to the field — this is the case where the force is largest and Fleming's left-hand rule applies directly.
strings.b-28.steps.2.title: Apply Fleming's left-hand rule
strings.b-28.steps.2.detail: Point the first finger along the magnetic field and the second finger along the current (opposite to the electron's motion). The thumb then gives the direction of the force, which is perpendicular to both the field and the current.
strings.b-28.steps.3.title: Read the answer from the figure
strings.b-28.steps.3.detail: Carrying this out for the directions shown gives a force directed into the page.
strings.b-28.answer: Option (d): the force is directed into the page.
strings.b-30.question: A positively-charged particle (alpha-particle) projected towards west is deflected towards north by a magnetic field. The direction of magnetic field is
strings.b-30.explanation: The particle is positive, so the current is towards the west. The force is towards the north, at right angles to the current. Applying Fleming's left-hand rule to these two directions, the first finger (field) must point upward.
strings.b-31.question: In the experiment with the aluminium rod AB hanging between the poles of a horse-shoe magnet, the rod is displaced towards the left when current is passed through it from end B to end A. What happens if the direction of the current through the rod is reversed?
strings.b-31.options.0: It is displaced towards the right.
strings.b-31.options.1: It is displaced towards the left.
strings.b-31.options.2: It is not displaced at all.
strings.b-31.options.3: It is displaced upwards, along the field.
strings.b-31.explanation: The direction of the force on the rod is reversed when the direction of the current through the conductor is reversed. So the rod is displaced in the opposite direction, towards the right.
strings.b-32.question: You are sitting in a chamber with your back to one wall. An electron beam, moving horizontally from the back wall towards the front wall, is deflected by a strong magnetic field to your right side. The direction of the magnetic field is
strings.b-32.explanation: The electrons move from the back wall to the front wall, so the direction of current is taken opposite to their motion, from the front wall towards the back wall. The beam is deflected to your right, so the force is to the right. Applying Fleming's left-hand rule to these two directions, the first finger must point vertically downward.
strings.b-33.question: When is the force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field largest?
strings.b-33.options.0: When the current is parallel to the magnetic field.
strings.b-33.options.1: When the current is at right angles to the magnetic field.
strings.b-33.options.2: When the current in the conductor is zero.
strings.b-33.options.3: When the conductor is placed along the field lines.
strings.b-33.explanation: The displacement of the rod is largest, that is, the force is highest, when the direction of the current is at right angles to the direction of the magnetic field.
strings.b-34.question: Which rule gives the direction of the force experienced by a current-carrying straight conductor placed in a magnetic field perpendicular to it?
strings.b-34.options.3: the rule of like and unlike poles
strings.b-34.explanation: Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor: first finger along the field, second finger along the current, thumb along the force. The right-hand thumb rule (Maxwell's corkscrew rule) is for the direction of the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor.
strings.b-35.paragraphs.0: In our homes we receive supply of electric power through a main supply, either supported through overhead electric poles or by underground cables. One of the wires in this supply, usually with red insulation cover, is called the live wire, or positive wire. Another wire, with black insulation, is called the neutral wire, or negative wire. In our country the potential difference between the two is 220 V, and we receive AC electric power of 220 V with a frequency of 50 Hz.
strings.b-35.paragraphs.1: At the meter-board in the house, these wires pass into an electricity meter through a main fuse. Through the main switch they are connected to the line wires in the house. These wires supply electricity to separate circuits within the house. Often two separate circuits are used: one of 15 A current rating for appliances with higher power ratings such as geysers and air coolers, and the other of 5 A current rating for bulbs, fans, etc.
strings.b-35.paragraphs.2: The earth wire, which has insulation of green colour, is usually connected to a metal plate deep in the earth near the house. This is used as a safety measure, especially for those appliances that have a metallic body, for example an electric press, toaster, table fan or refrigerator. The metallic body is connected to the earth wire, which provides a low-resistance conducting path for the current. Thus it ensures that any leakage of current to the metallic body of the appliance keeps its potential to that of the earth, and the user may not get a severe electric shock.
strings.b-36.caption: A schematic of a common domestic circuit. The red-insulated live wire and the black-insulated neutral wire come from the mains through a fuse, the electricity meter and the main switch. The bulb and the metal-bodied appliance are connected in parallel across the two wires, each with its own switch, and the metal body of the appliance is joined to the green-insulated earth wire that ends at a metal plate in the earth.
strings.b-37.paragraphs.0: In each separate circuit, different appliances can be connected across the live and neutral wires, and each appliance has a separate switch to switch the current through it on and off. In order that each appliance has equal potential difference, they are connected in parallel to each other.
strings.b-37.paragraphs.1: An electric fuse is an important component of all domestic circuits. A fuse in a circuit prevents damage to the appliances and the circuit due to overloading. Overloading can occur when the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact. This happens when the insulation of wires is damaged or there is a fault in the appliance. In such a situation the current in the circuit abruptly increases. This is called short-circuiting.
strings.b-37.paragraphs.2: The use of an electric fuse prevents the electric circuit and the appliance from a possible damage by stopping the flow of unduly high electric current. The Joule heating that takes place in the fuse melts it and breaks the electric circuit. Overloading can also occur due to an accidental hike in the supply voltage, and sometimes by connecting too many appliances to a single socket.
strings.b-39.question: Name two safety measures commonly used in electric circuits and appliances.
strings.b-39.options.0: the fuse and the earth wire
strings.b-39.options.2: the electricity meter and the fuse
strings.b-39.explanation: The fuse breaks the circuit when the current becomes too large, and the earth wire gives a low-resistance path so that a leakage current to a metallic body does not give a severe shock.
strings.b-40.question: What precaution should be taken to avoid the overloading of domestic electric circuits?
strings.b-40.options.0: Connect as many appliances as possible to one socket.
strings.b-40.options.1: Do not connect too many appliances to a single socket.
strings.b-40.options.2: Remove the fuse from the circuit.
strings.b-40.options.3: Use wires whose insulation is damaged.
strings.b-40.explanation: Overloading can be caused by connecting too many appliances to a single socket, so the number of appliances on one socket must be kept small. An accidental hike in the supply voltage can also overload a circuit.
strings.b-41.question: At the time of short circuit, the current in the circuit
strings.b-41.explanation: In a short circuit the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact, so the current in the circuit abruptly increases.
strings.b-42.question: State whether the following statements are true or false: (a) The field at the centre of a long circular coil carrying current will be parallel straight lines. (b) A wire with a green insulation is usually the live wire of an electric supply.
strings.b-42.explanation: At the centre of a long circular coil the arcs of the field circles appear as straight lines, so (a) is true. The green-insulated wire is the earth wire; the live wire has red insulation, so (b) is false.

lesson.title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
objectives: After this lesson you can describe the magnetic field of a magnet and its field lines, and list the properties of field lines.
After this lesson you can find the direction of the magnetic field produced by a current in a straight wire, in a circular loop and in a solenoid, using the right-hand thumb rule.
After this lesson you can use Fleming's left-hand rule to find the direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field.
After this lesson you can describe the wires, the safety devices and the common faults of a domestic electric circuit.

sections.title: Electricity and magnetism are linked
paragraphs: A current in a wire can heat the wire, but it can do something else too. A wire carrying an electric current behaves like a magnet.

To see this, connect a straight thick copper wire between two points X and Y of a circuit, keeping the wire perpendicular to the plane of the paper. Place a small compass horizontally near the wire and note where its needle points. Then insert the key and pass a current. The needle is deflected.
The deflection means that the electric current through the copper wire has produced a magnetic effect. So electricity and magnetism are linked to each other.

Hans Christian Oersted, one of the leading scientists of the 19th century, found this in 1820. He accidentally discovered that a compass needle got deflected when an electric current passed through a metallic wire placed nearby. Through this observation he showed that electricity and magnetism were related phenomena. The unit of magnetic field strength is named the oersted in his honour.

sections.title: Magnetic field and field lines
paragraphs: A compass needle gets deflected when brought near a bar magnet. A compass needle is, in fact, a small bar magnet: its ends point approximately towards north and south. The end pointing towards north is called the north-seeking or north pole, and the other end, pointing towards south, is the south-seeking or south pole.

Fix a sheet of white paper on a drawing board and place a bar magnet at the centre. Sprinkle iron filings uniformly around the magnet and tap the board gently. The filings arrange themselves in a pattern. The magnet exerts its influence in the region surrounding it, so the filings experience a force and line up. The region surrounding a magnet, in which the force of the magnet can be detected, is said to have a magnetic field. The lines along which the iron filings align themselves represent magnetic field lines.

Magnetic field is a quantity that has both direction and magnitude. The direction of the magnetic field at a point is taken to be the direction in which a north pole of the compass needle moves inside it. So by convention, field lines emerge from the north pole and merge at the south pole. Inside the magnet the direction of field lines is from its south pole to its north pole. Thus magnetic field lines are closed curves.

The relative strength of the magnetic field is shown by the degree of closeness of the field lines. The field is stronger, that is, the force acting on the pole of another magnet placed there is greater, where the field lines are crowded. Along a field line, the deflection of the compass needle increases as the needle is moved towards the poles.
No two field lines cross each other. If they did, it would mean that at the point of intersection the compass needle would point towards two directions, which is not possible.

Very weak magnetic fields are present in our bodies too. Ion currents along nerve cells produce temporary fields about one-billionth of the earth's magnetic field. The heart and the brain produce significant fields, and the magnetic field inside the body is the basis of getting images of body parts by a technique called Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI).

sections.title: Magnetic field due to a current through a straight conductor
paragraphs: Pass a current through a long straight thick copper wire held vertically, and sprinkle iron filings uniformly on a cardboard through which the wire passes. Tapping the cardboard gently makes the filings arrange themselves in a pattern of concentric circles around the copper wire. These circles represent the magnetic field lines.

Place a compass at a point on one of the circles. The direction of the north pole of the compass needle gives the direction of the field line at that point, and you can show it with an arrow. Reversing the current through the wire reverses the direction of the field lines.

Vary the current and watch the deflection. If the current is increased, the deflection also increases. This shows that the magnitude of the magnetic field produced at a given point increases as the current through the wire increases.

Now keep the current the same and move the compass farther from the wire. The deflection decreases. So the magnetic field produced by a given current in the conductor decreases as the distance from it increases, and the concentric circles representing the field become larger and larger as we move away from the wire.

sections.title: The right-hand thumb rule
paragraphs: Here is a convenient way to find the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying straight conductor. Imagine that you are holding the conductor in your right hand such that your thumb points towards the direction of the current. Then your fingers wrap around the conductor in the direction of the field lines of the magnetic field. This is known as the right-hand thumb rule.

The same rule is also called Maxwell's corkscrew rule. If you imagine driving a corkscrew in the direction of the current, then the direction of rotation of the corkscrew is the direction of the magnetic field.

sections.title: Magnetic field due to a current through a circular loop and a solenoid
paragraphs: Bend the straight wire into a circular loop and pass a current through it. The magnetic field produced by a current-carrying straight wire depends inversely on the distance from it, so at every point of the loop the circles representing the magnetic field become larger and larger as we move away from the wire. By the time we reach the centre of the loop, the arcs of these big circles appear as straight lines. Every point on the wire contributes a field that appears as a straight line at the centre of the loop. By applying the right-hand rule, every section of the wire contributes to the field lines in the same direction within the loop.

The magnetic field produced by a current-carrying wire at a given point depends directly on the current passing through it. So if a circular coil has n turns, the field produced is n times as large as that produced by a single turn. This is because the current in each circular turn has the same direction, and the field due to each turn then just adds up.

A solenoid is a coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wound in the shape of a cylinder. Its magnetic field lines are like those of a bar magnet: one end of the solenoid acts as a magnetic north pole. The field lines inside the solenoid are parallel straight lines, and the magnetic field is the same at all points inside a long solenoid carrying current. A strong magnetic field inside a current-carrying solenoid magnetises a piece of steel placed inside it, and this arrangement is called an electromagnet.

sections.title: Force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field
paragraphs: A current flowing through a conductor produces a magnetic field, and that field exerts a force on a magnet placed near the conductor. Andre Marie Ampere suggested that the magnet must also exert an equal and opposite force on the current-carrying conductor.

To see this, suspend a small aluminium rod AB, about 5 cm long, horizontally from a stand using two connecting wires. Place a strong horse-shoe magnet so that the rod lies between its two poles with the magnetic field directed upwards: the north pole vertically below and the south pole vertically above the rod. Connect the rod in series with a battery, a key and a rheostat, and pass a current through the rod from end B to end A. The rod is displaced. Reverse the direction of the current, and the rod is now displaced in the opposite direction.

So the direction of the force on the conductor depends upon the direction of the current and the direction of the magnetic field. Change either one of them and the direction of the force is reversed. The displacement of the rod is largest, that is, the magnitude of the force is the highest, when the direction of the current is at right angles to the direction of the magnetic field.

In that case a simple rule gives the direction of the force. It is called Fleming's left-hand rule. Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of your left hand so that they are mutually perpendicular. If the first finger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the second finger in the direction of the current, then the thumb will point in the direction of motion, or the force acting on the conductor.
Devices that use current-carrying conductors and magnetic fields include the electric motor, the electric generator, loudspeakers, microphones and measuring instruments.

sections.title: Domestic electric circuits
paragraphs: In our homes we receive electric power through a main supply, supported either through overhead electric poles or by underground cables. The wire with red insulation is called the live wire, or positive wire. The wire with black insulation is called the neutral wire, or negative wire. In our country the potential difference between the two is 220 V, and the supply is AC electric power of 220 V with a frequency of 50 Hz.

At the meter-board in the house these wires pass into an electricity meter through a main fuse, and through a main switch they are connected to the line wires in the house. These wires supply electricity to separate circuits within the house. Often two separate circuits are used: one of 15 A current rating for appliances with higher power ratings such as geysers and air coolers, and the other of 5 A current rating for bulbs, fans, etc.

The earth wire has insulation of green colour and is usually connected to a metal plate deep in the earth near the house. It is used as a safety measure, especially for appliances that have a metallic body, for example an electric press, toaster, table fan or refrigerator. The metallic body is connected to the earth wire, which provides a low-resistance conducting path for the current. Thus any leakage of current to the metallic body of the appliance keeps its potential at that of the earth, and the user may not get a severe electric shock.

In each separate circuit, different appliances can be connected across the live and neutral wires, and each appliance has a separate switch. They are connected in parallel to each other so that each appliance has the same potential difference.

An electric fuse is an important component of all domestic circuits. A fuse prevents damage to the appliances and the circuit due to overloading. Overloading can occur when the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact, which happens when the insulation of wires is damaged or there is a fault in the appliance. In such a situation the current in the circuit abruptly increases; this is called short-circuiting. The Joule heating that takes place in the fuse melts it and breaks the electric circuit, stopping the flow of the unduly high current. Overloading can also occur due to an accidental hike in the supply voltage, and sometimes by connecting too many appliances to a single socket.

A coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wound in the shape of a cylinder; its field is like that of a bar magnet and is uniform inside.

A safety device that melts by Joule heating and breaks the circuit when the current is too large.

The electric current through the wire has produced a magnetic effect.
The compass needle has lost its magnetism.
The current in the wire has stopped.

spec.question: Why does a compass needle get deflected when brought near a bar magnet?
options: The needle is a small bar magnet, and the magnetic field of the bar magnet exerts a force on it.
The bar magnet heats the needle.
Air pressure pushes the needle aside.
The needle becomes electrically charged.
spec.answer: The needle is a small bar magnet, and the magnetic field of the bar magnet exerts a force on it.
spec.explanation: A compass needle is itself a small bar magnet. Inside the magnetic field of the bar magnet it experiences a force, so it turns and its ends point along the field lines.
spec.expected_understanding: A compass needle is a small bar magnet and lines up with the magnetic field at its position.

spec.question: Which one of the following is NOT a property of magnetic field lines?
options: They emerge from the north pole and merge at the south pole.
They are crowded where the magnetic field is stronger.
They cross one another near the poles.
They form closed curves.
spec.answer: They cross one another near the poles.
spec.explanation: No two field lines are found to cross each other. If they did, then at the point of intersection the compass needle would point towards two directions at the same time, which is not possible.
spec.expected_understanding: Field lines never intersect; crowding shows relative strength; lines are closed curves.

spec.title: How to draw a magnetic field line with a compass

steps.title: Fix the paper and the magnet
steps.detail: Place a bar magnet on a sheet of white paper fixed on a drawing board, and mark the boundary of the magnet.

steps.title: Start near the north pole
steps.detail: Place the compass near the north pole of the magnet. The south pole of the needle points towards the magnet's north pole, and the needle's north pole is directed away from it.

steps.title: Mark the needle
steps.detail: Mark on the paper the position of the two ends of the needle.

steps.title: Move the needle onwards
steps.detail: Move the compass to a new position such that its south pole occupies the position previously occupied by its north pole.

steps.title: Walk to the south pole
steps.detail: Go on step by step in this way till you reach the south pole of the magnet.

steps.title: Join the marks
steps.detail: Join the points marked on the paper by a smooth curve. This curve represents a field line. Repeat the whole procedure and draw as many lines as you can.

paragraphs: Pass a current through a long straight thick copper wire held vertically, and sprinkle iron filings uniformly on a cardboard through which the wire passes. paragraphs: What happens to the deflection of a compass needle placed at a given point if the current in the copper wire is changed? Vary the current and watch. If the current is increased, the deflection also increases. This indicates that the magnitude of the magnetic field produced at a given point increases as the current through the wire increases.

What happens if the compass is moved away from the copper wire while the current stays the same? Place the compass at a farther point. The deflection in the needle decreases. Thus the magnetic field produced by a given current in the conductor decreases as the distance from it increases, and the concentric circles representing the field around a current-carrying straight wire become larger and larger as we move away from it.

spec.question: Which of the following correctly describes the magnetic field near a long straight wire?
options: The field consists of straight lines perpendicular to the wire.
The field consists of straight lines parallel to the wire.
The field consists of radial lines originating from the wire.
The field consists of concentric circles centred on the wire.
spec.answer: The field consists of concentric circles centred on the wire.
spec.explanation: Iron filings sprinkled on a cardboard through which the wire passes settle along concentric circles around the wire, so the field lines near a long straight current-carrying wire are concentric circles centred on the wire.
spec.expected_understanding: The shape of the field pattern of a straight current-carrying wire.

spec.question: In the activity with a straight copper wire lying parallel to and over a compass needle, the current flows from north to south and the north pole of the needle moves towards the east. The current is now made to flow from south to north. The north pole of the needle will move towards the
options: east.
west.
north.
south.
spec.answer: west.
spec.explanation: Reversing the direction of the current through the wire reverses the direction of the magnetic field produced by it, so the needle is deflected the opposite way — towards the west.
spec.expected_understanding: The direction of the magnetic field reverses when the current is reversed.

paragraphs: Here is a convenient way of finding the direction of the magnetic field associated with a current-carrying conductor. Then your fingers will wrap around the conductor in the direction of the field lines of the magnetic field. This is known as the right-hand thumb rule.

This rule is also called Maxwell's corkscrew rule. If we consider ourselves driving a corkscrew in the direction of the current, then the direction of the rotation of the corkscrew is the direction of the magnetic field.

Use it like this: first fix the direction of the current with your thumb, then read the direction of the field from the way your fingers curl. The field circles lie in planes perpendicular to the wire.

spec.problem: A current through a horizontal power line flows in east to west direction. What is the direction of magnetic field at a point directly below it and at a point directly above it?

steps.title: Note the direction of the current
steps.detail: The power line is horizontal and the current flows from east to west.

steps.title: Apply the right-hand thumb rule
steps.detail: Hold the wire in your right hand with the thumb pointing along the current, from east to west. Your fingers then curl around the wire in the direction of the magnetic field.

steps.title: Picture the field circles
steps.detail: The field lines are circles lying in a plane perpendicular to the wire, that is, in a vertical plane running north-south. The field at a point directly below the wire and at a point directly above the wire both lie on these circles.

steps.title: Read off the sense of turning
steps.detail: Looking along the wire from the east end, the curling of the fingers — and so the field — turns clockwise; looking from the west end, the same field turns anti-clockwise.

spec.answer: The magnetic field at any point below or above the wire turns clockwise in a plane perpendicular to the wire when viewed from the east end, and anti-clockwise when viewed from the west end.

spec.question: A long straight wire carries a current vertically upwards. Using the right-hand thumb rule, the magnetic field lines around the wire are
options: straight lines parallel to the wire.
circles around the wire, running anticlockwise when seen from above.
circles around the wire, running clockwise when seen from above.
radial lines spreading out from the wire.
spec.answer: circles around the wire, running anticlockwise when seen from above.
spec.explanation: Point the thumb of your right hand upwards along the current; your fingers curl around the wire. Seen from above, that curl is anticlockwise.

By the time we reach the centre of the circular loop, the arcs of these big circles appear as straight lines. Every point on the wire carrying current gives rise to a magnetic field that appears as a straight line at the centre of the loop. Applying the right-hand rule, it is easy to check that every section of the wire contributes to the magnetic field lines in the same direction within the loop.

spec.question: A circular loop of wire lies in the plane of the table and the current flows clockwise when seen from above. The magnetic field at the centre of the loop is
options: in the plane of the table, pointing outwards from the centre.
perpendicular to the table, pointing downwards into the table.
perpendicular to the table, pointing upwards.
zero at the centre of the loop.
spec.answer: perpendicular to the table, pointing downwards into the table.
spec.explanation: Apply the right-hand rule to the loop: curl your fingers in the direction of the current, which is clockwise seen from above, and the thumb points away from you — downwards into the table. So the field inside the loop is perpendicular to the table, pointing downwards, and outside the loop it points the other way.
spec.expected_understanding: Using the right-hand rule to find the direction of the field inside and outside a current-carrying loop.

paragraphs: The magnetic field produced by a current-carrying wire at a given point depends directly on the current passing through it. Therefore, if there is a circular coil having n turns, the field produced is n times as large as that produced by a single turn. This is because the current in each circular turn has the same direction, and the field due to each turn then just adds up.

A solenoid is a coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wound in the shape of a cylinder. Its magnetic field lines are like those of a bar magnet: one end of the solenoid acts as a magnetic north pole. The field lines inside the solenoid are parallel straight lines, and the magnetic field is uniform — the same at all points — inside a long solenoid carrying current.

A strong magnetic field inside a current-carrying solenoid is used to magnetise a piece of steel placed inside it. An electromagnet consists of a core of soft iron wrapped around with a coil of insulated copper wire.

spec.question: Choose the correct option. The magnetic field inside a long straight solenoid carrying current
options: is zero.
decreases as we move towards its end.
increases as we move towards its end.
is the same at all points.
spec.answer: is the same at all points.
spec.explanation: The field lines inside a long current-carrying solenoid are parallel straight lines, evenly spaced, so the field is uniform — the same at all points inside it.
spec.expected_understanding: The field inside a long solenoid is uniform.

paragraphs: An electric current flowing through a conductor produces a magnetic field, and the field so produced exerts a force on a magnet placed in the vicinity of the conductor. The French scientist Andre Marie Ampere suggested that the magnet must also exert an equal and opposite force on the current-carrying conductor.

Suspend a small aluminium rod AB, about 5 cm long, horizontally from a stand using two connecting wires. Place a strong horse-shoe magnet so that the rod lies between the two poles with the magnetic field directed upwards: the north pole vertically below and the south pole vertically above the rod. Connect the rod in series with a battery, a key and a rheostat, and pass a current through the rod from end B to end A. The rod is displaced. Reverse the direction of the current and the rod is displaced in the opposite direction.

Now interchange the two poles of the magnet so that the field is vertically downwards. Once again the direction of the force acting on the current-carrying rod gets reversed. This shows that the direction of the force on the conductor depends upon the direction of the current and the direction of the magnetic field.

Experiments have shown that the displacement of the rod is largest, that is, the magnitude of the force is the highest, when the direction of the current is at right angles to the direction of the magnetic field. In such a condition we can use a simple rule to find the direction of the force on the conductor.

The rule is Fleming's left-hand rule. Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of your left hand such that they are mutually perpendicular. If the first finger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the second finger in the direction of the current, then the thumb will point in the direction of motion, or the force acting on the conductor.
Devices that use current-carrying conductors and magnetic fields include the electric motor, the electric generator, loudspeakers, microphones and measuring instruments.

spec.caption: Fleming's left-hand rule. The three directions are mutually perpendicular: the first finger points along the magnetic field, the second finger along the current, and the thumb along the force (or motion) on the conductor.

spec.problem: An electron enters a magnetic field at right angles to it. The direction of force acting on the electron will be (a) to the right. (b) to the left. (c) out of the page. (d) into the page.

steps.title: Fix the direction of the current
steps.detail: The direction of current is taken opposite to the direction of motion of electrons. So first turn the electron's direction of motion round by half a turn to get the direction of the current.

steps.title: Note the angle between current and field
steps.detail: The electron enters at right angles to the field, so the current is also at right angles to the field — this is the case where the force is largest and Fleming's left-hand rule applies directly.

steps.title: Apply Fleming's left-hand rule
steps.detail: Point the first finger along the magnetic field and the second finger along the current (opposite to the electron's motion). The thumb then gives the direction of the force, which is perpendicular to both the field and the current.

steps.title: Read the answer from the figure
steps.detail: Carrying this out for the directions shown gives a force directed into the page.

spec.answer: Option (d): the force is directed into the page.

spec.question: A positively-charged particle (alpha-particle) projected towards west is deflected towards north by a magnetic field. The direction of magnetic field is
options: towards south
towards east
downward
upward
spec.answer: upward
spec.explanation: The particle is positive, so the current is towards the west. The force is towards the north, at right angles to the current. Applying Fleming's left-hand rule to these two directions, the first finger (field) must point upward.
spec.expected_understanding: Using Fleming's left-hand rule with a positive charge, where the current is along the motion.

spec.question: In the experiment with the aluminium rod AB hanging between the poles of a horse-shoe magnet, the rod is displaced towards the left when current is passed through it from end B to end A. What happens if the direction of the current through the rod is reversed?
options: It is displaced towards the right.
It is displaced towards the left.
It is not displaced at all.
It is displaced upwards, along the field.
spec.answer: It is displaced towards the right.
spec.explanation: The direction of the force on the rod is reversed when the direction of the current through the conductor is reversed. So the rod is displaced in the opposite direction, towards the right.
spec.expected_understanding: Reversing the current through a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field reverses the direction of the force.

spec.question: You are sitting in a chamber with your back to one wall. An electron beam, moving horizontally from the back wall towards the front wall, is deflected by a strong magnetic field to your right side. The direction of the magnetic field is
options: vertically upward
vertically downward
towards the back wall
towards the front wall
spec.answer: vertically downward
spec.explanation: The electrons move from the back wall to the front wall, so the direction of current is taken opposite to their motion, from the front wall towards the back wall. The beam is deflected to your right, so the force is to the right. Applying Fleming's left-hand rule to these two directions, the first finger must point vertically downward.
spec.expected_understanding: Current is opposite to electron motion, and Fleming's left-hand rule gives the field direction when the force and current directions are known.

spec.question: When is the force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field largest?
options: When the current is parallel to the magnetic field.
When the current is at right angles to the magnetic field.
When the current in the conductor is zero.
When the conductor is placed along the field lines.
spec.answer: When the current is at right angles to the magnetic field.
spec.explanation: The displacement of the rod is largest, that is, the force is highest, when the direction of the current is at right angles to the direction of the magnetic field.
spec.expected_understanding: The force is largest for current at right angles to the field.

spec.question: Which rule gives the direction of the force experienced by a current-carrying straight conductor placed in a magnetic field perpendicular to it?
options: the right-hand thumb rule
Fleming's left-hand rule
Maxwell's corkscrew rule
the rule of like and unlike poles
spec.answer: Fleming's left-hand rule
spec.explanation: Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor: first finger along the field, second finger along the current, thumb along the force. The right-hand thumb rule (Maxwell's corkscrew rule) is for the direction of the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor.
spec.expected_understanding: Distinguish the rule for the field of a current from the rule for the force on a current in a field.

paragraphs: In our homes we receive supply of electric power through a main supply, either supported through overhead electric poles or by underground cables. One of the wires in this supply, usually with red insulation cover, is called the live wire, or positive wire. Another wire, with black insulation, is called the neutral wire, or negative wire. In our country the potential difference between the two is 220 V, and we receive AC electric power of 220 V with a frequency of 50 Hz.

At the meter-board in the house, these wires pass into an electricity meter through a main fuse. Through the main switch they are connected to the line wires in the house. These wires supply electricity to separate circuits within the house. Often two separate circuits are used: one of 15 A current rating for appliances with higher power ratings such as geysers and air coolers, and the other of 5 A current rating for bulbs, fans, etc.

The earth wire, which has insulation of green colour, is usually connected to a metal plate deep in the earth near the house. This is used as a safety measure, especially for those appliances that have a metallic body, for example an electric press, toaster, table fan or refrigerator. The metallic body is connected to the earth wire, which provides a low-resistance conducting path for the current. Thus it ensures that any leakage of current to the metallic body of the appliance keeps its potential to that of the earth, and the user may not get a severe electric shock.

paragraphs: In each separate circuit, different appliances can be connected across the live and neutral wires, and each appliance has a separate switch to switch the current through it on and off. In order that each appliance has equal potential difference, they are connected in parallel to each other.

An electric fuse is an important component of all domestic circuits. A fuse in a circuit prevents damage to the appliances and the circuit due to overloading. Overloading can occur when the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact. This happens when the insulation of wires is damaged or there is a fault in the appliance. In such a situation the current in the circuit abruptly increases. This is called short-circuiting.

The use of an electric fuse prevents the electric circuit and the appliance from a possible damage by stopping the flow of unduly high electric current. The Joule heating that takes place in the fuse melts it and breaks the electric circuit. Overloading can also occur due to an accidental hike in the supply voltage, and sometimes by connecting too many appliances to a single socket.

spec.question: Name two safety measures commonly used in electric circuits and appliances.
options: the fuse and the earth wire
the switch and the bulb
the electricity meter and the fuse
the rheostat and the switch
spec.answer: the fuse and the earth wire
spec.explanation: The fuse breaks the circuit when the current becomes too large, and the earth wire gives a low-resistance path so that a leakage current to a metallic body does not give a severe shock.
spec.expected_understanding: The two safety devices of a domestic circuit and what each does.

spec.question: What precaution should be taken to avoid the overloading of domestic electric circuits?
options: Connect as many appliances as possible to one socket.
Do not connect too many appliances to a single socket.
Remove the fuse from the circuit.
Use wires whose insulation is damaged.
spec.answer: Do not connect too many appliances to a single socket.
spec.explanation: Overloading can be caused by connecting too many appliances to a single socket, so the number of appliances on one socket must be kept small. An accidental hike in the supply voltage can also overload a circuit.
spec.expected_understanding: One cause of overloading and the precaution against it.

spec.question: At the time of short circuit, the current in the circuit
options: reduces substantially.
does not change.
increases heavily.
varies continuously.
spec.answer: increases heavily.
spec.explanation: In a short circuit the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact, so the current in the circuit abruptly increases.

spec.question: State whether the following statements are true or false: (a) The field at the centre of a long circular coil carrying current will be parallel straight lines. (b) A wire with a green insulation is usually the live wire of an electric supply.
options: Both (a) and (b) are true.
(a) is true and (b) is false.
(a) is false and (b) is true.
Both (a) and (b) are false.
spec.answer: (a) is true and (b) is false.
spec.explanation: At the centre of a long circular coil the arcs of the field circles appear as straight lines, so (a) is true. The green-insulated wire is the earth wire; the live wire has red insulation, so (b) is false.
spec.expected_understanding: The field at the centre of a coil, and the colour code of domestic wires.

spec.question: What is the function of an earth wire, and why is it necessary to earth metallic appliances?
options: It carries the working current to the appliance.
It provides a low-resistance conducting path, so a leakage of current to a metallic body keeps the body's potential at that of the earth and the user may not get a severe electric shock.
It raises the potential difference supplied to the appliance.
It melts and breaks the circuit when the current is too large.
spec.answer: It provides a low-resistance conducting path, so a leakage of current to a metallic body keeps the body's potential at that of the earth and the user may not get a severe electric shock.
spec.explanation: Metallic appliances are earthed because their bodies can touch a leaking current. The earth wire gives that current an easy path to the earth, so the body stays at the earth's potential and the user is protected.
spec.expected_understanding: The purpose of the earth wire for metal-bodied appliances.

spec.question: Which two of these are methods of producing a magnetic field?
options: using a magnet and using a current-carrying conductor
using a fuse and using an earth wire
using a switch and using a bulb
using a rheostat and using a voltmeter
spec.answer: using a magnet and using a current-carrying conductor
spec.explanation: A magnetic field exists in the region around a magnet, and a metallic wire carrying an electric current also has a magnetic field around it. These are the two ways of producing a magnetic field described in this chapter.
spec.expected_understanding: Magnetic fields come from magnets and from electric currents.
